column5: Adam takes and eats the forbidden fruit
column6: Genesis depicts Adam's first transgression as eating fruit in the woman's temptation scene rather than naming forgetfulness; it is the necessary biblical counter-narrative to the commentary's Adam of Q 20:115 who forgets and lacks resolve.

column5: written Torah read continually to learn fear
column6: The king keeps a written Torah with him and reads it all his days in order to fear YHWH and keep its words, concentrating the commentary's book, recitation, retention, and fear motifs in one scene.

column5: word near in mouth and heart
column6: The word's nearness in Israel's mouth and heart for doing it gives a compact Torah formulation for revelation that is both recited and inwardly held.

column5: write on tablet and book for a future day
column6: Isaiah is told to inscribe the testimony so it endures as a witness for the future, a specific biblical reason to preserve prophetic speech in writing.

column5: former scroll restored with additional words
column6: After the burning, Baruch writes the former words from Jeremiah's mouth and many similar words are added; this distinct final step makes remembered speech both recoverable and expandable in a new scroll.

column5: God gives each according to ways and deeds
column6: YHWH's searching judgment and recompense according to each person's ways supplies a Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's cited earlier-sheet ethics of personal effort and return.

column5: every deed brought into judgment
column6: The final judgment of every hidden good or evil deed adds the judicial outcome to the commentary's 53:38-42 sequence of individual burden, effort, and return to God.

column5: God gives Moses divinely written tablets to teach
column6: Jubilees opens by having God give Moses tablets of law and commandment already written for teaching Israel, a Second Temple expansion of the Mosaic written-revelation scene.

column5: Moses read in synagogues every Sabbath from ancient generations
column6: James describes Moses as publicly read every Sabbath in city synagogues, a New Testament witness to the continuing recitation of an ancient Mosaic written legacy.

column5: an orderly written account follows received tradition
column6: After the eyewitness delivery described in Luke 1:2, the author writes an orderly account; the verse supplies the distinct written outcome of the oral transmission already in view.

column5: hearers hold the word fast in a good heart
column6: In the good-soil explanation, hearers retain the word and bear fruit with endurance, a precise Christian image for held rather than dropped revelation.

column5: Jesus' words will not pass away
column6: The contrast of passing heaven and earth with imperishable words is a direct New Testament counterpart to the commentary's passing worldly life and retained divine speech.

column5: the Lord's word endures and is preached
column6: The Petrine reuse of the enduring-word formula identifies that lasting word with the gospel preached to its readers, combining permanence and proclamation.

column5: name not erased from the book of life
column6: The promise not to erase the conqueror's name gives a Christian book-image for being retained before God, alongside the commentary's contrast between forgetting and divine record.

column5: each person gives an account to God
column6: Paul's formula of each person giving an account of self directly reinforces the individual accountability the commentary attributes to the earlier sheets.

column5: Job desires his words inscribed permanently
column6: Job's wish that his words be written in a book makes durable inscription the response to threatened loss in a non-prophetic setting, extending the commentary's concern with pages that hold what speech might otherwise lose.

column5: seal the book until the time of the end
column6: Daniel is told to keep the words secret and seal the book until the end; its guarded, delayed access provides a qualified inverse to 87:6's enabled recital and 87:18's available earlier sheets.

column5: Moses' authorship and the catalog of biblical books
column6: The rabbinic discussion that attributes Moses' book and other works to named authors is a later Jewish way of organizing the textual corpus behind the commentary's named Mosaic pages.

column5: one hundred versus one hundred and one reviews
column6: The contrast between reviewing a lesson one hundred and one times versus one hundred times supplies a rabbinic practice of repetition aimed at preventing the loss the commentary calls forgetting.

column5: Papias prefers the living voice to information from books
column6: Papias' reported preference for remembered living testimony over books gives a Christian counter-emphasis: the commentary joins memory to sheets, whereas this reception tradition privileges living recall over written repositories.

column5: written teaching and unwritten apostolic tradition
column6: Basil distinguishes church teaching received from writing from teaching transmitted through unwritten apostolic tradition, a later Christian framework that complicates any simple equation of preserved revelation with pages alone.
